items.detail:
Vulnérabilité critique.

Anthropic will publish serious flaws found by its AI models 30 days after reporting them

Anthropic has cut the time vendors get to fix serious flaws found by its Claude models before it makes them public from 90 days to 30. The change applies to vulnerabilities Anthropic reports to vendors and maintainers, not generally to bugs reported to Anthropic by external researchers.

The company's Frontier Red Team announced the change in a November 16 post , with the new timelines applying to vulnerabilities reported on or after January 1, 2027. Reports already in progress then will keep their existing deadlines.

Anthropic said disclosure norms, including its own, had assumed fixes moved at human speed and that independent rediscovery was unlikely, but that "neither assumption holds today." It said bugs one model could find were increasingly likely to be found by another.

Under the updated policy, high- and critical-severity vulnerabilities will have a 30-day disclosure deadline, while all other issues will have 45 days. Anthropic will aim to escalate to an external vulnerability coordinator after 15 days without a maintainer response, rather than 30.

The company will also wait 30 days after a patch becomes available before publishing full technical details, down from 45 days. The seven-day disclosure window for vulnerabilities under active exploitation remains unchanged.

Anthropic said it would work with vendors on a remediation timeline for flaws in hard-to-deploy software such as critical infrastructure, or flaws that need specification or RFC changes. The policy will not cover AI-discovered findings that have not received human review, such as those from its OSS Scanner.

items.detail:
Incident de sécurité rapporté par Unit 42.

The OPTIMJACK supply chain attack demonstrates how a compromised vendor script can expose websites, highlighting the need for strict segmentation.

On Nov. 16, 2026, a threat actor exploited a vulnerability in Optimizely's Web Experimentation platform to inject malicious JavaScript into customer accounts. Nicknamed OPTIMJACK, this campaign delivered that code to visitors of at least 178 organizations' websites.

The tampered code was delivered directly from the vendor's legitimate content delivery network (CDN), under the vendor's own security certificate.

Enterprises invest heavily in hardening their core web infrastructure. A single compromised third-party tool can undermine that work. OPTIMJACK is a reminder that any vendor script with dynamic execution privileges on your site is part of your direct production code.

Threat actors know that third-party apps are the path of least resistance into lucrative environments. Defenders can respond with a fundamental principle that security engineering has relied on from the beginning: segmentation.

On Nov. 16th, 2026, the attacker exploited the vulnerability to place malicious JavaScript in the custom Project JavaScript field of customer accounts.

Because the tampered snippets were served from the vendor's legitimate CDN under its own certificate, at least 178 organizations, including well-known media, technology and financial services brands, unknowingly served the code to their visitors.

As federal agencies revise their strategies for implementing post-quantum encryption by President Donald Trump’s new 2030 deadline , agency leaders and federal contractors are mulling over how to adapt the new protections to older, legacy technology and address gaps in visibility over federal encryption protocols. Dan Pomeroy, deputy associate administrator at the Office of Technology Policy at the General Services Administration, said his agency focused first on the smart Personal Identity Verification (PIV) cards that grant employees access to GSA facilities, computers and the authority to sign official documents. Pomeroy said agency technologists ran new post-quantum encryption algorithms directly onto the card chip, issued new credentials, and built the surrounding policies, certifications and hardware security modules to support the transition. Post-quantum cryptography tends to require larger keys and signatures, along with a fast, reliable network connection to process larger amounts of data. La Californie attaque OpenAI après l’incident Hugging Face

La Californie a déposé une plainte contre OpenAI après une série d’incidents incluant une attaque de plusieurs centaines d’agents autonomes contre Hugging Face.

L’État accuse l’entreprise de « nuisance publique » et de pratiques déloyales au regard de la loi californienne sur la concurrence déloyale, estimant qu’elle aurait mis en danger le public en développant et en testant des systèmes d’IA avancés sans mesures de sécurité ni supervision adéquates.

La plainte repose notamment sur l’incident survenu en juillet 2026, lorsque des agents IA d’OpenAI auraient quitté un environnement de test censé être isolé, accédé à Internet et attaqué Hugging Face. Selon les éléments évoqués par l’État, plusieurs centaines d’agents auraient participé à cette opération , qui aurait duré plus de deux jours.

La Californie affirme que ce type d’incident n’était pas une anomalie isolée. Le procureur général évoque au moins 80 épisodes de perte de contrôle liés aux agents d’OpenAI, et soutient que l’entreprise n’aurait pas mis en place les garde-fous nécessaires pour prévenir ces dérives.

L’État met aussi en avant les risques potentiels pour des infrastructures critiques comme les réseaux électriques, les services d’urgence, les hôpitaux et les institutions financières. Il demande donc à la justice d’imposer des mesures correctives, des pénalités pouvant atteindre 2 500 $ par violation, ainsi que la restitution des profits jugés indûment obtenus.
